questions: Who is the producer, and who eats it?
What do decomposers do at every link?
segments.say: Build the chain with me. Grass the producer first, then the rabbit that eats it - the primary consumer - then the fox, the secondary consumer. Decomposers work on every link when things die. Point at each role on your student notes as it appears.

questions: If producers hold 1000 units, about how much reaches the fox?
Where does the rest of the energy go?
segments.say: Now follow the energy. Only about a tenth of the energy at each level passes up - the rest is lost as heat. That shrinking share is why the pyramid narrows and why top carnivores are rare. Now try the energy question on your worksheet.

questions: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
Name two sources that put it back.
segments.say: Carbon takes a different path: it loops. Plants absorb carbon dioxide in photosynthesis - that is a sink. Animals return it by respiration, and decomposers feed the soil - those are sources. Trace one carbon atom round with your finger.

questions: What is lost when a forest is cleared?
segments.say: Humans can tip this balance. A forest stores carbon; deforestation clears that sink and carbon dioxide piles up in the air, warming the planet. Replanting pushes back by rebuilding the sink.

questions: Say the difference between the energy path and the nutrient path in one sentence.
Does energy ever get back to the grass?
segments.say: A common mistake mixes the two patterns up. Check your student notes and finish the exit ticket, keeping the flow and the loop separate.
segments.watchFor: Energy is recycled around the food chain like nutrients are. Listen for students who say the grass gets its energy back from the chain. Send them back to scene 2: Energy is not recycled: only about a tenth passes to the next level, the rest is lost as heat.
